match.reason: No bank point covers pyramids or cones; the closest cards handle prisms, cylinders and general surface area, which do not teach the base plus triangular faces method or the cone's slant height formula.

draft.title: Surface area of pyramids and cones
card: Its surface area is the area of the base plus the area of all its triangular faces. Find each face separately, then add.
Its curved surface has area \(\pi r l\), where \(r\) is the radius and \(l\) is the slant height. The slant height runs along the surface from the tip to the edge of the base.
The height, the radius and the slant height form a right-angled triangle, with \(l\) the longest side. So \(l^{2} = r^{2} + h^{2}\).

A cone has radius 3 cm and height 4 cm. Then \(l = \sqrt{3^{2} + 4^{2}} = 5\) cm, so the curved surface is \(\pi \times 3 \times 5 = 15\pi \text{ cm}^{2}\), about 47.1 square centimetres. Add the base \(\pi r^{2}\) for the total.
draft.remember: Pyramid: base plus triangles. Cone: curved part \(\pi r l\), with \(l\) from Pythagoras.

a.q: A cone has radius 5 cm and slant height 13 cm. What is the area of its curved surface?
a.why: Curved surface is \(\pi r l = \pi \times 5 \times 13 = 65\pi \text{ cm}^{2}\). The option \(90\pi\) adds the base \(25\pi\) as well, but the question asks only for the curved surface.
a.clue: Multiply the radius by the slant height, then by \(\pi\).

b.q: A cone has radius 6 cm and height 8 cm. What is the area of its curved surface?
b.why: The slant height is \(l = \sqrt{6^{2} + 8^{2}} = \sqrt{100} = 10\) cm, so the curved surface is \(\pi \times 6 \times 10 = 60\pi \text{ cm}^{2}\). Using the height 8 in place of the slant height gives \(48\pi\), which is the tempting mistake.
b.clue: Find the slant height with Pythagoras first.

wants.brief: A cone with its height h drawn from the tip straight down to the centre of the base, the radius r along the base, and the slant height l along the side from the tip to the edge of the base. A right-angled triangle formed by h, r and l is shown.
wants.why: It shows where the slant height sits and why Pythagoras' theorem finds it.
